title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We measured whether adding a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier (with at most one automated repair) increases the fraction of intent‑driven configuration proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Each pair evaluated a single shared LLM candidate under two conditions: baseline (accept single shot) and guarded (deterministic validation and ≤1 automated repair). Results: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.9966667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00,0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Under the supplied synthetic suite and model, single‑shot generation was near ceiling, limiting observable marginal rescue by the guarded pipeline. All preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts are archived with the study id to support replication and follow‑up experiments that vary estimand conditioning, model strength, or repair budget.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. Syntactic validity of an LLM output does not guarantee the semantic safety properties operators require (reachability, sequencing constraints, policy preservation). Prior work reports that generate→validate→repair scaffolds reduce some errors, but reported effect sizes vary with model capability, task hardness, and validator expressiveness. To quantify the deterministic rescue utility of a verifier and a bounded automated repair on identical LLM candidates, we preregistered and executed a paired experiment conditioning on a single shared_initial candidate per intent. The central research question is: does integrating a deterministic verifier (plus ≤1 automated repair) increase the probability that an LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation (unflagged) compared with accepting a single‑shot LLM output when both conditions evaluate the same candidate? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired evaluation (N=300 pairs) measuring verifier/repair rescue under a shared_initial estimand; (2) a fully archived execution and analysis bundle showing a near‑ceiling baseline for the selected synthetic suite and model; and (3) evidence‑grounded interpretation and operational guidance about estimand choice, near‑ceiling inference behavior, and reproducibility.
sections.related_work: Surveys and system papers demonstrate active interest in LLM applications for network management and propose tool‑augmented agentic frameworks that invoke external validators and repairs. Prior verified findings relevant to our positioning include: (a) LLMs can produce network configuration artifacts and intent translations but performance varies by task and dataset [https://openalex.org/W4406484968, https://openalex.org/W4411015066]; (b) planner‑centric and ReAct‑style tool‑augmented pipelines enable external validators to check semantics and steer repairs (e.g., planner‑centric proposals and tool‑use benchmarks) [doi:10.1609/aaai.v40i40.40676, https://openalex.org/W4389518608]; and (c) generate→validate→repair patterns often reduce errors when validator coverage aligns with operational constraints [https://openalex.org/W4416927413, https://openalex.org/W4404240614]. Limitations in prior work include heterogeneous benchmarks, variable validator expressiveness, and few controlled head‑to‑head comparisons that isolate verifier rescue from scaffold effects. Our study complements this literature by conditioning on the same LLM candidate per intent and thereby isolating the verifier/repair effect for that candidate rather than measuring gains from independent alternative model draws.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered study cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001 prior to the confirmatory run. The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) comparing guarded (validator + ≤1 repair) and baseline (accept single‑shot) conditions on the same shared_initial candidate. The preregistration (archived with the study id) specifies the design, inclusion/exclusion rules, analysis executor, and multiplicity plan.

Design choices and frozen parameters. Key frozen choices: model = gpt-5-mini; validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 executing the preregistered full_intent_constraint_validation rule; task suite = synthetic_topology_suite_v1 generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; per‑pair repair budget ≤1 automated repair call; shared_initial generation per pair (one model draw); planned analyzable pairs = 300 (100 per difficulty stratum: low/medium/high); maximum_model_calls = 600. The analysis executor is paired_binary_analysis_v1 implementing an exact two‑sided McNemar‑equivalent test and a paired bootstrap percentile CI (B = 10000, bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistration also specified a pilot (n = 60) for discordance estimation and power calibration.

Operationalization and scoring. Each pair used a single shared_initial LLM candidate which both conditions validated. Baseline: accept that candidate as the final proposal (no automated repair). Guarded: run the deterministic validator; if the validator flags the candidate, permit at most one automated repair attempt and then revalidate; pass/fail is determined by the validator's final verdict and the preregistered automated flagging rules. The deterministic validator checks sequencing constraints, reachability/policy invariants, and field‑level requirements according to the full_intent_constraint_validation rule. Episode scoring and validator traces were emitted deterministically and archived in the run bundle to allow exact replication of pass/fail decisions. The preregistration specified exclusion only if both pipeline calls for a pair failed due to provider/infrastructure outage; single-call failures would be handled per the executor's complete_pair_primary rule. (Pilot note: the preregistered pilot (n = 60) was not executed and no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed; the confirmatory N = 300 was used as pre‑specified.)
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter executed the confirmatory run: planned_episode_count = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions), completed_episode_count = 600, complete_pair_count = 300, model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared_initial + 1 repair). No pairs were excluded under the preregistered exclusion rules and no dual‑call provider outages occurred. Deterministic reconciliation recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and cache_miss_count = 301. The contamination summary is empty and the missingness summary records zero failed or unscorable episodes (analysis/missingness_summary.csv).

Primary outcomes and inferential results. Condition margins: baseline successes = 299/300 (0.9966667), guarded successes = 300/300 (1.0). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Confirmatory inference (paired_binary_analysis_v1) produced absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333, exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 (m = n10 + n01 = 1 discordant observation), and a 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00,0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Per‑stratum results: low = 100/100 baseline and guarded, medium = 100/100 baseline and guarded, high = baseline 99/100 vs guarded 100/100.

Rescued episode diagnostics. A single guarded episode invoked the permitted automated repair and produced the lone discordant pair (n10 = 1). The archived validator trace for that episode records that the validator detected a must_be_down_for_fields sequencing violation (the candidate lacked a required 'admin down' step prior to a VLAN/MTU change). The automated repair inserted the missing sequencing step; the subsequent revalidation returned valid == true. We report a concise semantic summary of the repair here; full validator traces and representative task manifests are archived in the run bundle for forensic inspection (manifested under execution/ and analysis/ artifacts).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation in a near‑ceiling regime. The LLM‑validator combination on the supplied synthetic suite produced a near‑ceiling baseline (99.7% single‑shot pass rate). With only one discordant pair among 300, the exact conditional McNemar test yields p = 1.0, which reflects insufficient discordant evidence rather than strong evidence that both conditions are identical in all settings. The paired bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01] bounds the plausible paired improvement under the shared_initial estimand to at most one percentage point in this experimental context. This behavior is typical when baseline success rates are near 100%: statistical power to detect small absolute improvements is limited by the number of discordant pairs rather than total N.

Estimand conditioning and operational meaning. The shared_initial design intentionally conditions on the same LLM candidate per intent; it therefore isolates the deterministic rescue/repair utility for that candidate. This estimand answers the operational question relevant to an organization that would apply a validator + bounded repair as an audit/repair layer after a single model draw. It does not measure verifier benefits that could arise from allowing independent alternative LLM draws per arm (e.g., verifier‑guided resampling, model steering, or iterative candidate generation). Interpreting null or near‑null discordance under shared_initial should therefore not be taken as evidence that validators are universally unnecessary; different estimands (independent draws, iterative repairs, larger repair budgets, or weaker LLMs) will change the measured effect.

Reproducibility and artifact grounding. All raw outputs, provider traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis CSVs (analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/missingness_summary.csv, analysis/contamination_summary.csv) are archived in the run bundle associated with the preregistration id. Representative task manifests and six example response traces are enumerated in the manuscript evidence bundle. The analysis executor parameters (bootstrap resamples, seed) and the exact inference method are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. Deterministic reconciliation confirms episode accounting and provider call audit counts; these artifacts allow an independent executor to reproduce the confirmatory calculations without manual reconstruction.

Operational implications and recommended follow‑ups. When base models are near‑ceiling relative to a chosen validator suite, a bounded verifier+repair (shared_initial) yields limited marginal correctness gain but still provides deterministic audit trails and targeted repair capability for localized sequencing or omission errors. To evaluate broader operational benefit, follow‑ups that are directly enabled by the archived artifacts should: (a) change the estimand to allow independent candidate draws per arm (to capture verifier–model interaction and guided resampling effects); (b) evaluate weaker LLMs or intentionally harder/realistic intents to increase discordance; and (c) expand the repair budget to iterative repairs or ensemble repair strategies and measure repair cost/benefit tradeoffs. The archived suite and manifests support these alternative analyses without fabricating new data.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired comparison between a verifier‑assisted pipeline (deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair) and accepting a single‑shot LLM candidate under the shared_initial estimand on 300 synthetic NetOps intents using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Baseline single‑shot generation achieved 299/300 unflagged verifier passes and the guarded pipeline 300/300, yielding an absolute paired improvement of 0.00333 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01]). These results demonstrate that measured verifier marginality depends strongly on base model capability, task difficulty, validator semantics, and estimand conditioning. We release the preregistration id, execution and analysis artifacts, representative task manifests, and validator traces in the archived run bundle to enable reproducible follow‑ups that vary estimand choice, model strength, or repair strategies.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated by the preregistered deterministic task generator; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase verifier marginal utility.
Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/diverse validators.

Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing limited discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements relative to larger pre‑specified targets.
Pilot not executed: the preregistered pilot intended for discordance estimation and power calibration was not run; no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions the estimand on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition.
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one automated repair per pair; larger or iterative repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
